extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters (city reporters) and copy/editors, especially those covering the church beat
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for writing fair, accurate, and newsworthy newspaper stories—with a focus on covering 'reformers' and the church beat (sermons, services, and related announcements). Emphasizes neutral wording, verification, balance, story structure, and managing sources/ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neutral wording; avoid loaded/connotative words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prejudicial or color words (e.g., 'threat', 'instigated', 'blast', 'compelled', 'smirked', 'sinners') that carry strong negative connotations and can put readers into a biased frame of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible pick less charged alternatives (e.g., 'caused' instead of 'instigated'). Beware that a single phrasing can bias readers; 'profaning' without quotes implies endorsement of the view. Watch verb choices like 'demanded' vs 'requested' and nouns/adjectives that imply malice or ridicule. Examples and paragraph-level annotations illustrate how particular words skew perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support quantified or comparative claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not state quantities or comparative claims (e.g., 'many condemnations' vs 'some support') unless they are supported or verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you claim numbers or frequencies, have the counts or clear sourcing. Otherwise use measured phrasing or attribute the claim. The text critiques the reporter for saying 'many' without counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying an official's stance without context
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'admitted, without enthusiasm' can mislead about an official's attitude unless the reporting provides the scene/details to justify that inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing a source's demeanor or position, provide concrete supporting detail (quotes, scene-setting) so readers can infer meaning, rather than asserting it yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use frequency statements that mislead by omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'rarely applied' are misleading if they omit relevant context (e.g., an ordinance only applies a limited time and therefore naturally is used less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why something occurs less frequently rather than letting a phrase imply neglect or dysfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain reporter impartiality; do not let personal dislike show
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must not allow personal prejudice against subjects (e.g., reformers) to influence tone, choice of words, or story emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-check for growing dislike (e.g., increasingly harsh descriptors, dropping honorifics) and correct wording to be fair and neutral. The piece gives examples of creeping bias and how it affects coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent, respectful use of titles and names
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep formality consistent (e.g., using 'the Rev. Mr. Halpin' throughout) to avoid signaling disrespect by suddenly using only a surname.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing from formal to familiar forms can reveal or create bias; maintain consistent naming conventions appropriate to the subject and the paper's style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal attacks; distinguish attacks on beliefs from attacks on person
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid printing comments that attack a person rather than critiquing their beliefs or actions (e.g., personal insults in the quotes) unless clearly newsworthy and contextualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal assaults are rarely good reporting; include them only when necessary and make clear they are opinion, not fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks and attributions correctly to avoid implied endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Using quoted words (or failing to quote) affects whether the story appears to endorse or condemn an expressed view (e.g., 'profaning' with or without quotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote precisely and attribute statements. Be careful that punctuation or lack of quotes doesn't make a subjective term appear authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance viewpoints and seek both sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on one side (e.g., golfers) and present a lopsided story; actively gather the opposing viewpoint and treat it with comparable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk to multiple sources representing differing perspectives; avoid letting late or minimal contact with one side produce an unbalanced narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair play test: willingness to show story to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical test for bias: if the reporter is willing to show the story to a member of the group written about before publication, the story is likely unbiased; reluctance indicates slant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-publication review (when appropriate) as a check for perceived unfairness. If unwilling to show, re-examine the story for slant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources offer suggestions but must not dictate wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters may weigh and accept useful suggestions from sources but should not let news sources determine how the story is written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept 'worthy suggestions' but retain editorial control. The reporter should not simply 'say it just the way I give it to you.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair play applies even to unpopular, eccentric, or minority groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when subjects are crackpots or unpopular minorities, treat them considerately and objectively; their narrowness will show through fair presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ridicule or slurring of political, racial, or religious minorities. Examples show how partisan phrasing degenerates coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and demonstrate the news value of a beat
rubrics_metrics.description: To revive or strengthen a beat (e.g., church beat), show readers consistently that there is news of high concern regularly in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'educate' readers into accepting news; demonstrate its relevance through regular, well-presented items across the beat's multiple facets (religious, social, intellectual, parental).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover sermons systematically; use volunteers/ministers as feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical method for covering many sermons is to arrange an automatic feed where ministers bring abstracts/sermons before a set deadline, ensuring regular and faithful coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set deadlines, guarantee placement if delivered on time, and use the ministers' self-interest to secure cooperation. Watch for pitfalls like reporter defection or ministerary defection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage ministers firmly and diplomatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Be politely brutal with ministers who fail to cooperate—if they don't bring sermons after repeated omission, they will resume cooperating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ministers expect the reporter to fetch sermons and then withdraw cooperation, persist in the policy that sermons must be delivered or they won't be printed; omission for several weeks typically restores cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify abstracts against actual sermons; get firsthand when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers sometimes tone down abstracts or diverge from notes; reporters should occasionally attend services or obtain the complete sermon to ensure accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If talk indicates abstracts differ from spoken sermons, go to the church for a few Sundays or request the full sermon text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not routinely accept ministers' written stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers sometimes offer to write the story; usually decline because they lack news judgment; accept only rarely when it is clearly worthwhile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let reporters craft the story; the minister's self-written piece may lack appropriate news values and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge sermon newsworthiness by interest, not congregation size
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermon placement and length should be determined by the degree to which it would interest all readers, not by the church's membership numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-church sermons that are dull need less space than small-church sermons that are powerful; avoid 'cast iron' judgments based solely on population or denomination dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional positive reinforcement to maintain cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes give a mediocre minister a somewhat generous story (but choose one of his better offerings) to show appreciation and encourage cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discretion: the purpose is to encourage continued participation, not to mislead readers about quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine church programs for non-sermon news and verify names
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements, membership lists, baptisms, forums, and programs often contain newsworthy items — but every name and fact must be verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs are a 'news mine'—prospect for items like large receptions or notable speakers; confirm spellings and details before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and context: do not pull remarks out of context
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers' utterances are under scrutiny; a minor aside (e.g., 'Sunday-morning golf is a worse peril...') must not be presented as the central theme if it was a brief digression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place quotes in context and proportion; if a sensational remark was a short aside, say so in the lead or avoid treating it as the main subject. Failure to contextualize is 'mercilessly unjust.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sermon stories with clear blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended story structure: Block 1 lead (sermon/other matter); Block 2 secondary lead; Block 3 catch-all; Block 4 amplification of Block 1; Block 5 amplification of Block 2; Block 6 lists/details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this block structure when a story highlights both sermons and other service elements. Examples show how to roll multiple sermons into a single story or separate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose roundup vs separate stories based on practical trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches: (a) one long roundup with a combined or dual lead (saves headlines and desk work but submerges many sermons); (b) separate story per sermon with individual headlines (gives each minister presence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider space, readability, and make-up desk workload when choosing. If space allows, lead a 'sermon page' with a roundup of the best sermons and separate stories for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Sundays: use mood stories and vivid but restrained color
rubrics_metrics.description: On major religious or temporal observances (Easter, Christmas, July 4), write longer, more descriptive 'mood' pieces that convey emotional response, but avoid overwriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill stories with color and feelings so readers can 'live over again' the service; be careful of excess and maintain focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware publicity-seeking preachers; assess real news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity-hungry ministers may make extravagant statements; don't automatically give them disproportionate space just because they're theatrical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust coverage to the sermon’s actual news value over time; once sensational preachers' impact wanes, scale back feature space accordingly.
